title: How toys move: rolling, bouncing, spinning and winding up

summary.text: A ball rolls down a slope, but a book stays put. A paper cup rolls too, yet it curves round in a circle instead of going straight. Your child tests what rolls, drops a ball from high and low, twists a string, spins a home-made top and pushes a book on pencils. They find that round things roll, that a rolling thing's own shape steers it, that a ball squashes and springs back when it bounces, and that a top stands up only while it spins. Every toy starts moving with a push or a pull, from a hand, a slope or a spring inside.
summary.art: A girl kneeling beside a chopping board leaned on books, watching a paper cup roll off it and curve round on the tiled floor, while a bottle rolls straight on.

intro.hook: Lean a tray on two books. Put a ball at the top and let go. Now put a book at the top and let go. What happens to each one?
intro.text: The ball rolled down. The book stayed where it was. Nobody pushed either of them. The slope gave them both the same chance. So why did only the ball move? In this unit you find out how toys move. Some roll, some bounce, some spin, and some wind up and go. You test each one with things from home.
intro.art: A tray leaned on two books, a red ball rolling off the bottom and a picture book sitting still at the top.

outcomes: By the end I can sort things that roll from things that slide or stay still, and say that round things roll.
By the end I can show that a rolling thing's shape steers it: a paper cup curves round, and a bottle goes straight.
By the end I can show that a ball squashes and springs back when it bounces, and never bounces as high as it fell from.
By the end I can show that a top spins round its middle, and stands up on its point only while it spins.
By the end I can say that winding a toy stores my push in a twist or a spring, and the toy gives it back as movement.
By the end I can say what push or pull starts a toy moving: a hand, a foot, a slope or a spring inside.

terms.meaning: To roll is to turn over and over while moving along.
terms.example: A ball rolls across the floor. A bottle on its side rolls down a slope.
terms.art: A ball rolling across a tiled floor, with little curved arrows showing it turning over and over.

terms.meaning: To slide is to move along while the same side keeps touching the ground.
terms.example: A book slides down a steep slope, flat side down. You slide on a smooth floor in socks.
terms.art: A book sliding down a steep tray, its flat side touching the tray all the way.

terms.meaning: A ball bounces when it hits the floor, squashes a little, springs back into shape and goes up again.
terms.example: A rubber ball bounces high on tiles. A ball of wet atta dough just goes splat and stays down.
terms.art: A rubber ball squashed flat on the floor, with arrows showing it springing back up.

terms.meaning: To spin is to turn round and round in one place, round your own middle.
terms.example: A top spins on its point. You spin when you turn round and round on the spot.
terms.art: A wooden top spinning on its point, with a dotted line showing the middle it turns round.

terms.meaning: A spring is a coil of metal that you can squash, stretch or wind, and it pushes back to its old shape.
terms.example: A wind-up toy has a spring inside. When you turn the key, the spring winds up tight. When you let go, it unwinds and turns the wheels.
terms.art: The inside of a wind-up toy car: a coiled metal spring joined to the wheels, and a key on the outside.

explanations.context: This card says why some things roll and others stay still or slide.
explanations.definition: A thing rolls when it is round where it touches the ground. A thing with a flat side stays still, or slides if the slope is steep.
explanations.description: On the slope, the ball, the bottle and the round pencil rolled. The book and the box stayed still. A ball is round all over, so a round part always touches the ground. A book has flat sides, so it cannot turn over. That is why wheels are round.
examples: In the slope test, the ball and the bottle rolled, and the book stayed still.
Car and cycle wheels are round, so they roll along the road.
A lumpy potato rolls a little, stops on a flat bit, then rolls again.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a ball rolling down a slope, and a book sitting still on the same slope.

explanations.concept: A rolling thing's shape steers it
explanations.context: This card says why the paper cup curved round, while the bottle went straight.
explanations.definition: A thing that is the same width all along, like a bottle, rolls straight. A thing that is wider at one end, like a cup, rolls round in a curve, towards its narrow end.
explanations.description: The bottle and the cup rolled down the same slope. The bottle went straight, and the cup curved round. The cup is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. On each turn the wide end goes a long way and the narrow end goes a short way, so the cup turns.
examples: In the slope test, the paper cup curved round, and the bottle rolled straight.
A tin of dal, the same width all along, rolls straight.
A steel tumbler that is wider at the top also curves when it rolls, but in a bigger circle.
explanations.art: A paper cup rolling in a curve on the floor, its wide end leaving a long dotted track and its narrow end a short one.

explanations.concept: A bounce is a squash and a spring back
explanations.context: This card says what happens to a ball when it bounces.
explanations.definition: When a ball hits the floor, it squashes a little. Then it springs back into its round shape, and that push sends it up again.
explanations.description: A rubber ball squashes for a moment when it hits the floor, too fast to see. Then it springs back into shape and pushes off the floor. A ball of atta dough squashes but does not spring back, so it stays down. A dropped ball never bounces as high as it fell from, because some of its movement turns into sound and a little warmth.
examples: In the drop test, the ball dropped from high up bounced higher than the ball dropped from low down.
The ball never came back up as high as the hand that dropped it.
A ball bounces well on hard tiles, and hardly at all on a soft pillow.
explanations.art: Three pictures of one ball: falling, squashed flat against the floor, and round again going up.

explanations.concept: A top stands up only while it spins
explanations.context: This card says why a top can stand on its point.
explanations.definition: A top stands up on its point while it spins fast. It falls over when it slows down and stops.
explanations.description: Try to stand a top on its point without spinning it. It falls over at once. Spin it, and it stands up on the same tiny point. As the point rubs on the floor, the spin slows, the top wobbles and falls. This rubbing is called friction.
examples: Your colour top fell over when it was still, and stood up while it spun.
A pambaram, the string top of Tamil Nadu, stands up while it spins and falls when it stops.
A spinning coin stands on its edge, then wobbles and falls flat as it slows.
explanations.art: Two tops: one still and fallen on its side, and one spinning upright on its point.

explanations.context: This card says how a wind-up toy or a twisted string keeps your push for later.
explanations.definition: When you wind a toy or twist a string, you give it a push that it keeps in a twist or a spring. When you let go, the twist or spring undoes itself, and the toy moves.
explanations.description: You twisted the string ten times. When you let go, the sock spun as the string untwisted, and twenty twists made it spin for longer. A wind-up toy works the same way. Turning the key winds a metal spring tight, and when you let go, the spring unwinds and turns the wheels. When the spring has unwound all the way, the toy stops.
examples: In Twist and Let Go, more twists made the sock spin for longer.
A pull-back car goes further when you pull it back further.
An old wall clock stops if nobody winds its key.
explanations.art: A hand turning the key of a wind-up toy, and a cut-away picture of the spring coiling up tight inside.

agreed.text: Every toy starts moving with a push or a pull.
agreed.evidence: A ball rolls when a hand or a slope starts it. A top spins when fingers or a string turn it. A wind-up toy moves when its spring, wound by your hand, pushes the wheels.

agreed.text: A dropped ball never bounces back as high as it was dropped from.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it by a wall. Scientists have measured it: on each bounce, some movement turns into sound and warmth.

agreed.text: Rubbing, called friction, slows down every rolling and spinning thing.
agreed.evidence: A top spins longer on a smooth plate than on a rough mat. A ball rolls further on tiles than on a carpet.

challenging.claim: A wind-up toy moves all by itself.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: Once you let go, nobody is touching the toy, and it still runs across the floor.
challenging.against: The toy runs only after you wind it, and stops when the spring has unwound. Wind it twice, and it goes a short way. Wind it many times, and it goes far. Your push was kept in the spring.
challenging.context: This card is about whether wind-up toys move on their own.

challenging.claim: A spinning top stays up because the air holds it.
challenging.for: Something must hold the top up, and the air is all around it.
challenging.against: Spinning wheels called gyroscopes keep spacecraft steady out in space, where there is no air. What keeps a top up is its spin, not the air.
challenging.context: This card is about what holds a spinning top up.

challenging.claim: The heavier the ball, the higher it bounces.
challenging.who: A guess many children and grown-ups make
challenging.for: A heavy ball hits the floor harder, so it seems it should jump back higher.
challenging.against: A light rubber ball bounces high, and a heavy ball of wet dough does not bounce at all. What matters most is whether the ball springs back into shape.
challenging.context: This card is about whether weight makes a ball bounce higher.

big_questions.q: The paper cup curved round on the floor. Could you make a cup that rolls straight?
big_questions.hint: What made it curve? What if both ends were the same width?

big_questions.q: A ball never bounces as high as it fell from. Where does the rest of its movement go?
big_questions.hint: Listen to a bounce. Feel a ball after bouncing it many times on the floor.

big_questions.q: The Earth spins round too, like a top. Why don't we feel it spinning?
big_questions.hint: Think of sitting in a smooth train with your eyes shut. Can you tell it is moving?

big_questions.q: Children in every country play with balls and tops. Why do you think people everywhere love things that roll and spin?
big_questions.hint: What do you feel when you watch a top spin?

story.title: The Cup That Went to Ammamma
story.note: Tara, Kiran and Ammamma are made up. Ammamma means grandmother in Malayalam and in Telugu. Etikoppaka, a village in Andhra Pradesh, really is famous for its painted wooden toys, including tops.
text: Tara was seven. She lived in a flat in Kochi with her little brother Kiran and their grandmother, Ammamma.
It was the monsoon. Rain drummed on the windows all afternoon, and nobody could go out to play.
'Let's make a slope,' said Ammamma. She leaned the big wooden chopping board on a pile of books.
Kiran fetched his red ball. He put it at the top of the board and let go. The ball rolled down, across the floor, all the way to the door.
'Now my book!' said Kiran. He put his picture book at the top and let go. It just sat there.
'It's stuck,' said Kiran, frowning.
'Look at its sides,' said Tara. 'The book is flat. The ball is round all over. Round things roll.'
Kiran found a water bottle and laid it on its side at the top. Off it went, straight down the board and straight across the floor to the door.
Then Tara had an idea. She fetched a paper cup from the kitchen. 'Where will this go?' she asked.
'To the door, like the bottle,' said Kiran.
Tara let go. The cup rolled down the board. But on the floor it did not go to the door. It curved away, round and round, and stopped by Ammamma's feet.
Kiran laughed. 'It is going to Ammamma!'
They tried again. Again the cup curved round. 'Why does it do that?' asked Kiran.
Ammamma held up the cup. 'Look at its two ends,' she said. 'One is wide and one is narrow.'

Tara rolled the cup slowly along the floor with her hand. She watched both ends. 'The wide end goes a long way on each turn,' she said. 'The narrow end goes only a little way. So the cup turns round, like a cart with one big wheel and one small wheel.'
Kiran looked at the bottle. 'The bottle is the same at both ends,' he said slowly. 'So it goes straight.'
'You two worked it out yourselves,' said Ammamma, and she smiled.
Then she opened her old tin box. Inside was a wooden top, painted red and yellow. 'My grandmother bought me this in Etikoppaka, when I was as small as you,' she said.
Kiran tried to stand the top on its pointed end. It fell over at once. He tried again. It fell again.
Ammamma wound a string round the top. She threw it down and pulled the string back. The top landed on its point and spun, standing up straight, humming on the floor.
'It's standing up!' said Kiran.
'Only while it spins,' said Tara. 'Watch.'
The top spun slower and slower. It began to wobble. Then it tipped over and rolled in a little circle on its side.
That evening, Kiran looked at the two paper cups on the shelf. 'Could we make a cup that goes straight?' he asked.
'Try it tomorrow,' said Ammamma. 'You know what steers a cup now.'
Kiran nodded. 'Both ends must be the same,' he said slowly. Then he went to find the tape.
Ammamma clapped, and Tara wrote it in her science book.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Tara and Kiran find that round things roll and flat things stay still. The paper cup curves round because its wide end goes further on each turn than its narrow end, while a bottle, the same at both ends, rolls straight. Kiran works out that a straight-rolling cup needs both ends the same, and your child can test that in the challenge. The top stands on its point only while it spins.
ask: Why did the book stay at the top of the slope, when the ball rolled?
Why did the paper cup curve round to Ammamma, instead of going to the door?
When could the top stand up on its point?
What does Kiran think a cup needs, to roll straight?
art: A girl and her little brother in a flat on a rainy day, a chopping board leaned on books, and a red ball rolling to the door.
A paper cup curving round on the floor towards a smiling grandmother's feet.
A red and yellow wooden top spinning upright on the floor, a grandmother holding the string.
A boy holding two paper cups and a roll of tape, with a paper cup and a bottle on the floor beside him.

experiments.title: Roll, Stay or Slide? The slope test
experiments.context: In this experiment you lean a tray on books to make a slope. You let go of eight things at the top, one at a time, without pushing. You sort them by what they do. You watch where a bottle and a paper cup go when they reach the floor. Last, you make the slope steeper to see when a book starts to slide.
experiments.question: Which things will roll down the slope, and which will stay still or slide? Will a paper cup roll the same way as a bottle? How steep must the slope be before a book slides?
experiments.predict: Guess first, for each thing. Will it roll, stay still, or slide? Will the cup go straight like the bottle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same slope for every thing. We put each thing at the top and let go, without any push. We try the bottle and the cup twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: My guess: roll, stay or slide?

materials.item: a tray, a big chopping board or a large hardback book, for the slope
4 thick books, to lift one end of the slope (use 2 at first)
a small ball
an empty plastic water bottle with straight sides, lid on
a round pencil or a round marker pen
a small box, such as a matchbox or a toothpaste box
an eraser or a flat steel spoon
an onion or a small potato
a picture book
a paper cup or a plastic cup, wider at the top than the bottom
a sheet of paper and a crayon, for the results

schedule.what: Make the slope, guess, let go of each thing, sort them, watch the bottle and the cup on the floor, then make the slope steeper until the book slides.

experiments.record: Look at your folded paper. Each thing is now in the part where it belongs. Draw the ones you did not draw yet.

setup.art: A tray leaned on two thick books on a tiled floor, with a clear space on the floor in front of it.
setup.caption: 1. Lean a tray on books to make a slope.

setup.art: A child's hand holding a ball at the top of the tray, ready to let go, and a box, an onion, a pencil and a cup waiting beside.
setup.caption: 2. Put one thing at the top. Let go. Don't push.

setup.art: A paper with three parts, headed by a little ball, a little box and a little sliding book, with drawings of things in each part.
setup.caption: 3. Sort each thing: roll, stay or slide.

setup.art: A bottle rolling straight across a tiled floor, and a paper cup curving round in a circle beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Watch the bottle and the cup on the floor.

setup.art: A tray leaned steeply on four books, a picture book sliding down it with its flat side touching the tray.
setup.caption: 5. Make the slope steeper. When does the book slide?

flow.do: 1. Lean the tray on two books on a bare floor. 2. Clear about two big steps of floor in front of it. 3. Put the eight things beside the slope. Keep the other two books handy. 4. Fold the sheet of paper into three parts. Draw a ball, a box and a sliding book at the top of the parts.
flow.say: Here is our slope. We will put each of these things at the top and let go. We won't push them at all.
flow.kid: Look at the slope. Look at all the things. We will let go of each one.
flow.parent: Bare tiles or stone work best. A carpet stops things too soon.

flow.do: Hold up each thing. Ask your child to guess: roll, stay or slide. Put each thing in a guess pile.
flow.say: Look at this onion. When I let go at the top, will it roll, stay still or slide? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Will it roll, stay or slide? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the ball will roll?
good: It is round.
Balls always roll.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen. The reasons matter most.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts each thing at the top and lets go, without pushing. 2. Watch what it does. 3. Try each thing once more if you like. 4. Put it on the part of the folded paper where it belongs: roll, stay or slide.
flow.say: Put it at the very top. Now open your fingers and let go. No pushing! What did it do? Let's try it once more.
flow.kid: Put it at the top. Let go. No push. What did it do?

ask.q: Which things rolled? What is the same about them?
good: The ball, the bottle and the pencil rolled. They are round.
The round ones rolled.

flow.parent: The ball, the bottle and the round pencil should roll. The box, the eraser and the book usually stay still. The onion may roll a little and stop.

flow.do: 1. Lay the bottle on its side at the top. 2. Ask: where will it go on the floor? 3. Let go and watch. 4. Do the same with the cup lying on its side. 5. Try the bottle and the cup twice each.
flow.say: The bottle and the cup are both round. When they reach the floor, will they go the same way? Why do you think so? Let's watch.
flow.kid: Will the bottle and the cup go the same way? Why? Watch.

ask.q: What did the cup do on the floor?
good: It went round in a circle.
It curved. The bottle went straight.

flow.parent: The bottle rolls straight on. The cup curves round in a circle on the floor. If the cup rolls off the side of the tray, put it in the middle and try again.

flow.do: 1. Put the picture book at the top of the slope. 2. Lift the top end of the tray with one more book. 3. Let go of the picture book. 4. Add one more book each time, until the picture book slides. 5. Count the books.
flow.say: The book stayed still on our first slope. How many books do you think we need under the tray before it slides? Let's add one at a time and see.
flow.kid: Add a book under the tray. Let go of the picture book. Does it slide yet?

ask.q: What did the steeper slope do to the book?
good: It slid down.
The steep slope made it slide, but it did not roll.

flow.parent: The book slides with its flat side down, and does not roll. If it still stays after all four books, try the flat steel spoon or the matchbox instead.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: What did you find out? Which things rolled? Why did the cup go round, and the bottle go straight?
flow.kid: What rolled? Why did the cup go round?

good: One end is big and one end is small.
The wide end goes further.

check.q: Meenakshi, a girl aged seven, lets go of a book and a ball at the top of a slope. What happens?
options: The ball rolls, and the book stays still
The book rolls, and the ball stays still
check.why: A ball is round all over, so it rolls. A book has flat sides, so it stays still, or slides if the slope is steep.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own words first. Then say it plainly: round things roll. The cup's wide end goes further on each turn than its narrow end, so the cup turns. The bottle is the same at both ends, so it goes straight.

experiments.title: High Drop, Low Drop: how high will the ball bounce?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop a ball beside a wall, once from knee height and once from a grown-up's shoulder. A grown-up marks how high it bounces back each time.
experiments.question: Will a ball dropped from high up bounce higher than one dropped from low down? Will it ever bounce back as high as your hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which drop will make the higher bounce? Will the ball come back up to your hand? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same ball and the same floor each time. We let go of the ball, without throwing it. We drop it three times from each height, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: My guess: high or low bounce?
How high it bounced (where the bindi is)

materials.item: a rubber ball, a plastic ball or a tennis ball that bounces well
a bare wall beside a hard floor
4 bindis, or small bits of paper and sticky tape, to mark the wall

schedule.what: Mark two drop heights on the wall, drop the ball three times from each, and mark how high it bounces.

experiments.record: Draw the wall, the two drop marks and the two bounce marks. Draw an arrow down from each drop mark, and an arrow up to its bounce mark.

setup.art: A wall with one bindi at a child's knee height and one at a grown-up's shoulder height, and a ball on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Mark two drop heights on the wall.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a ball at shoulder height beside the wall and letting go, while a child crouches to watch the bounce.
setup.caption: 2. Let go of the ball. Don't throw it.

setup.art: The grown-up pressing a bindi on the wall at the top of the bounce, below the shoulder mark.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the top of the bounce.

flow.do: 1. Stick one bindi on the wall at your child's knee height. 2. Stick another at your own shoulder height.
flow.say: These two bindis are where we will drop the ball from. One is low, at your knee. One is high, at my shoulder.
flow.kid: Look at the two bindis. One is low. One is high.
flow.parent: A plain wall next to a tiled floor is best. Keep away from glass and the TV.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before any drops.
flow.say: When we drop the ball from up here, will it bounce higher than from your knee? Will it come right back up to my hand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: High drop or low drop: which bounces higher? Why?

good: From high up it hits the floor harder.
It will come back to the hand.

flow.do: 1. Drop the ball from the knee bindi three times. 2. Your child watches the top of the bounce. 3. Stick a bindi there. 4. Do the same from the shoulder bindi.
flow.say: Watch the very top of the bounce, where the ball stops and turns round. Point to it. I'll put a bindi there.
flow.kid: Watch the top of the bounce. Point to it.

ask.q: Which drop made the higher bounce?
good: The high one.
From your shoulder it bounced much higher.

flow.parent: Let go of the ball. Don't throw it down. Your child crouching at the side sees the top of the bounce best. The marks will not be exact, and that is fine.

flow.do: Look at all four bindis together. Ask your child what they see.
flow.say: Look at the shoulder bindi and the bounce bindi under it. Did the ball ever come back up to my hand?
flow.kid: Did the ball come back up to the hand?

ask.q: Did the ball come back as high as it fell from?
good: No, always a bit lower.
It never got back to the hand.

flow.do: Ask what your child found, and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: What did you find out? Where did the rest of the ball's movement go? Listen when it bounces.
flow.kid: What did you find? What do you hear when it bounces?

check.q: Kavya, a girl aged eight, drops a ball from the height of her head. How high will it bounce back?
options: Not as high as her head
Exactly as high as her head
check.why: A dropped ball never bounces back as high as it fell from. On each bounce, some of its movement turns into sound and a tiny bit of warmth.

flow.parent: Say it plainly after your child's own words: a higher drop gives a higher bounce, but the ball never comes back to the hand. Some movement goes into the sound of the bounce.

activities.title: Toy Hunt: how does each toy move?
activities.context: In this activity you gather five toys or home things. You make each one move, and say how it moves and what started it.

materials.item: 5 toys or home things that move, such as a ball, a toy car, a top, a bangle and a doll

schedule.what: Gather five toys, make each one move, and say how it moved and what started it.

activities.record: Draw three of your toys. Next to each one, draw a hand, a foot or a slope to show what started it moving.

setup.art: A ball, a toy car, a wooden top, a bangle and a cloth doll laid out on a mat.
setup.caption: 1. Gather five toys.

setup.art: A girl pushing a toy car with her hand, and a parent holding up a ball, ready to drop it.
setup.caption: 2. Make each one move. Say how it moved.

flow.do: Ask your child to bring five toys or things that move. Lay them on the floor.
flow.say: Bring me five toys that can move. Let's lay them out here.
flow.kid: Bring five toys that move. Put them here.

flow.do: Your child makes each toy move. For each one, ask how it moved and what started it.
flow.say: How does this one move? Does it roll, bounce, spin or slide? What started it moving: your hand, your foot or a slope?
flow.kid: Make it move. Does it roll, bounce, spin or slide? What started it?

ask.q: What started the toy car moving?
good: My hand pushed it.
I pushed it, and then it rolled.

flow.parent: A bangle on its edge rolls. A doll slides or falls. Some toys do two things: a ball can roll and bounce.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is one more toy to think about.
flow.kid: Think about this toy.

check.q: Divya, a girl aged seven, has a toy car lying still on the floor. What will make it move?
check.why: A still toy stays still until a push or a pull starts it moving.

activities.title: Twist and Let Go: a string that winds up
activities.context: In this activity you hang a sock on a string, twist it round and round, and let go. You find out what more twists do.

materials.item: a string, about as long as your arm
a sock with a small ball or a rolled-up hanky inside, tied to one end of the string

schedule.what: Twist the hanging sock ten times and let go, then twenty times, and watch how long it spins.

activities.record: Draw the sock hanging on the string. Draw curly arrows round it to show it spinning.

setup.art: A girl holding a string up high, with a stuffed sock hanging from the end, and a parent turning the sock round and round to twist the string.
setup.caption: 1. Twist the sock round and round.

setup.art: The sock spinning fast on the string, with curly arrows round it, and the girl watching.
setup.caption: 2. Let go of the sock. Watch it spin.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string to the sock with the ball inside. 2. Your child holds the top of the string up high, arm still.
flow.say: Hold the string up high and keep your arm still. I will twist the sock round and round.
flow.kid: Hold the string high. Keep your arm still.

flow.do: 1. Turn the sock round ten times, counting aloud. 2. Ask what will happen. 3. Let go of the sock and watch.
flow.say: Ten twists. Now, what will the sock do when I let go? Why do you think so? Let's watch.
flow.kid: Count the ten twists. What will happen? Watch.

good: It spun round really fast.
It spun, then stopped, then spun the other way.

flow.parent: The sock spins fast as the string untwists. Then it often twists the string a little the other way, and spins back.

flow.do: Do it again with twenty twists. Count how long it spins.
flow.say: This time, twenty twists. Will it spin for longer or shorter? Count with me while it spins.
flow.kid: Now twenty twists. Will it spin longer? Count.

good: It spun for longer.
It went faster and longer.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: A wind-up toy has a spring inside that you twist with a key. What do you think more turns of the key will do?
flow.kid: Answer this one.

check.q: Zainab, a girl aged six, and her friend Lakshmi, aged seven, have the same kind of wind-up toy. Zainab winds hers with three turns. Lakshmi winds hers with ten turns. Whose toy goes further?
check.why: More turns wind the spring tighter. The toy gives back what you put in, so more winding makes it go further.

activities.title: Book on Rollers: push it on round pencils
activities.context: In this activity you push a heavy book across the floor with one finger. Then you put round pencils under it, and push again.

materials.item: a heavy book, such as a dictionary or a big school atlas
4 round marker pens or round pencils (not six-sided ones), all the same size
a smooth floor

schedule.what: Push a heavy book with one finger, then push it on four round pencils, and compare.

activities.record: Draw the book on the floor, and then the book on its pencils. Put a big arrow by the one that was easier to push.

setup.art: A girl pushing a fat dictionary across a tiled floor with one finger, looking like it is hard.
setup.caption: 1. Push the book with one finger.

setup.art: The same dictionary sitting on four round pencils laid side by side, and the girl pushing it easily.
setup.caption: 2. Put it on pencils. Push again.

flow.do: Your child pushes the heavy book across the floor with one finger.
flow.say: Push this book with just one finger. Is it easy or hard?
flow.kid: Push the book with one finger. Easy or hard?
flow.parent: If the book is easy to push, stack a few more books on it until one finger can only just move it.

flow.do: 1. Lay four round pencils side by side, a little apart. 2. Put the book on top. 3. Ask your child to guess. 4. Your child pushes with one finger.
flow.say: Now the book sits on round pencils. Will it be easier or harder to push? Why do you think so? Try it.
flow.kid: The book is on pencils now. Easier or harder? Why? Push.

good: The pencils rolled.
Round things roll, so the book rode on them.

flow.parent: The book glides easily as the pencils roll. Pencils come out at the back, so move them to the front to keep going. Rollers like this have been used to move heavy loads.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a question about a big box.
flow.kid: Answer this one.

check.q: Anjali, a girl aged seven, needs to move a heavy box across the floor. What would help most?
options: Putting a flat book under it
check.why: Round rods roll, so the box rides along on them. That is much easier than dragging it.

activities.title: Pull-Back Car: short pull, long pull
activities.context: This activity is for families who have a pull-back or wind-up toy car. You pull it back a short way and a long way, and see how far it goes. If you have no such toy, skip this and do Twist and Let Go.

materials.item: a pull-back or wind-up toy car
a smooth floor
2 chappals, to mark where the car stops

schedule.what: Pull the car back a little and a lot, let go, and mark where it stops each time.

activities.record: Draw the car and two chappals. Write or draw which pull went further.

setup.art: A boy pulling a small toy car backwards along a tiled floor with his hand pressing it down.
setup.caption: 1. Pull the car back, pressing it down.

setup.art: The car racing forward after he lets go, and a chappal marking where it stopped.
setup.caption: 2. Let go. Mark where it stops.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses the car down and pulls it back one hand length. 2. Let go. 3. Put a chappal where it stops.
flow.say: Pull it back just a little, one hand long. Let go. Where did it stop? Let's mark it.
flow.kid: Pull back a little. Let go. Mark where it stops.

flow.do: Now pull it back three hand lengths. Ask for a guess first, then let go and mark it.
flow.say: This time, three hands long. Will it go further or less far? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pull back a lot. Will it go further? Why?

ask.q: What did the longer pull do?
good: It went much further.
It went faster too.

flow.parent: Inside, the backwards pull winds a small spring. A longer pull winds it more, so the car goes further.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: What is inside the car that keeps your pull?
flow.kid: Answer this one.

check.q: What makes a pull-back car run forward when you let go?
options: A spring inside, wound up by your pull
The floor pushes it by itself
check.why: Pulling back winds a spring inside. When you let go, the spring unwinds and turns the wheels.

games.title: Roll, Bounce, Spin or Slide? The act-it-out card game
games.players: 2 or more players. One player is the caller, and you take turns.
games.context: This is a card game you act out. The caller reads a card. Every player, the caller too, acts out how the thing moves: roll on the mat, bounce on the spot, spin slowly, slide in socks, or drop down and stay still.

items.f: A football kicked along the ground
items.b: ROLL. It is round all over.

items.f: A rubber ball dropped on tiles
items.b: BOUNCE. It squashes and springs back up.

items.f: A top spun on the floor
items.b: SPIN. It turns round its middle.

items.f: A book on a steep slope
items.b: SLIDE. Its flat side stays on the slope.

items.f: A bangle let go on its edge
items.b: ROLL. It is round like a wheel.
SPIN. The blades turn round the middle.

items.f: A cycle going down the road
A child going down a playground slide
items.b: SLIDE. You slide down on your bottom.

items.f: A coin spun on a table
items.b: SPIN. It spins, then wobbles and falls.

items.f: A tennis ball thrown at a wall
items.b: BOUNCE. It springs back off the wall.

items.f: A steel plate pushed across the table
items.b: SLIDE. Its flat bottom slides along.

items.f: A ball of wet atta dough dropped on the floor
items.b: NONE OF THEM. It squashes and stays down.

rules: Mix the 12 cards and put them face down.
The caller reads the top card out loud. A grown-up reads for a caller who cannot read yet.
Everyone, the caller too, acts out the move: roll on a mat, bounce on the spot, spin slowly once, or slide in socks. If the card has none of these moves, drop down flat and stay still.
The caller turns the card over and reads the answer. Everyone who acted it out right and can say why gets a point.
Play until all 12 cards are read. The player with the most points wins. If points are tied, everyone wins. To play again, swap callers.

setup.art: A parent reading a card aloud, and two children ready to act on a mat.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: One child curled up rolling on a mat, and another bouncing on the spot with arms up.
setup.caption: 2. Act out how the thing moves.

flow.do: Read the rules. Practise each move together, slowly and safely.
flow.say: Show me roll: lie down and roll on the mat. Bounce: jump on the spot. Spin: turn round slowly once. Slide: glide in your socks. And if it is none of these, drop down flat and stay still.
flow.kid: Roll, bounce, spin, slide. Try each one.
flow.parent: Spin slowly, once, so nobody gets dizzy and falls. Slide only on a clear floor.

flow.do: Play all 12 cards. After each card, ask how the player knew.
flow.say: A bangle let go on its edge. Act it out! How did you know it rolls?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Act it out. Say how you know.

ask.q: How do you know the bangle rolls?
good: It is round like a wheel.
It turns over and over.

flow.parent: The reason matters more than the acting. Some things do more than one move: a ball can roll and bounce.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last card to think about.
flow.kid: Answer the last one.

check.q: A girl lets go of a round steel tumbler lying on its side on a slope. What will it do?
check.why: A tumbler on its side is round where it touches the slope, so it rolls.

games.title: Bottle Skittles: roll the ball, knock them down
games.context: This is a rolling game. You stand six empty bottles in a triangle and roll a ball at them from a line. Plastic cups or tumblers that stand up will do if you have no bottles.
rules: Stand 6 empty plastic bottles in a triangle: 3 at the back, then 2, then 1 at the front.
Lay a dupatta on the floor as the rolling line, about 3 big steps from the bottles.
Each player rolls a ball along the floor from the line. No throwing.
After each roll, count how many bottles fell. Write the number on your score sheet, or a grown-up writes it. Then stand all the bottles up again.
Each player has 3 rolls. Add up your 3 numbers, with a grown-up's help.
The player with the highest total wins. If two players tie, both win.

setup.art: Six empty plastic bottles standing in a triangle at the end of a corridor, and a dupatta on the floor as a line.
setup.caption: 1. Stand six bottles in a triangle.

setup.art: A girl crouching at the dupatta line, rolling a ball along the floor towards the bottles.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the ball from the line.

flow.do: Set up the bottles and the line. Show how to roll the ball, low along the floor.
flow.say: We roll the ball, we don't throw it. Keep your hand low, near the floor, and let go.
flow.kid: Roll the ball. Keep your hand low.

flow.do: Take turns. After a few rolls, ask what helps the ball go straight.
flow.say: Which rolls hit the most bottles? What did you do with your hand on those rolls?
flow.kid: Roll the ball. What helped it go straight?

ask.q: What helps the ball hit the bottles?
good: Rolling it straight from the middle.
A bigger push so it doesn't stop.

flow.parent: A bigger push sends the ball faster, so it knocks down more bottles. A ball let go at an angle rolls off to the side.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a question about the ball.
flow.kid: Answer this one.

check.q: Revathi, a girl aged seven, rolls her ball at the bottles, but it stops before it reaches them. What should she try?
check.why: A bigger push makes the ball roll faster and further before rubbing on the floor slows it down.

projects.title: Make a Colour Top
projects.context: In this project you make a top from a card circle and a short pencil. You colour it, spin it, and watch the colours change. You also try to stand it up without spinning.
projects.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the card with a sharp pencil point, pressing into an eraser or a lump of atta dough below.

materials.item: a piece of thin card from a cereal or sweet box
a steel katori or a small cup, to draw round
a short pencil about as long as your finger
crayons or sketch pens: red and yellow
child-safe scissors
a smooth plate or a tiled floor to spin it on

schedule.what: Make the card circle, colour it, push in the pencil, then spin it and try to stand it still.

projects.record: Draw your top before spinning. Then draw what the colours looked like while it spun.

setup.art: A child drawing round a steel katori on a piece of card with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round a katori on card. Cut out the circle.

setup.art: A card circle coloured half red and half yellow, with a short pencil pushed through the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Colour it. A grown-up pushes a short pencil through the middle.

setup.art: The top spinning on a steel plate, its colours blurred into orange.
setup.caption: 3. Spin it. Watch the colours.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws round the katori on the card. 2. Cut out the circle. 3. Find the middle by folding it in half twice and opening it.
flow.say: Draw round the katori. Now cut out the circle. Fold it in half, then in half again. Where the folds cross is the middle.
flow.kid: Draw round the katori. Cut it out. Fold it to find the middle.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours one half red and the other half yellow. 2. A grown-up makes a hole at the middle with a sharp pencil point. 3. Push the short pencil through, so a little of its point sticks out below.
flow.say: Colour one half red and one half yellow. Now I'll make a hole right in the middle, and push the pencil through.
flow.kid: Colour half red, half yellow. A grown-up makes the hole.
flow.parent: The hole must be at the very middle, or the top wobbles and falls at once. Keep the card about two finger-widths above the pencil point. If the card slips on the pencil, wrap a little tape round the pencil under the card.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries to stand the top on its point without spinning. 2. Then twist the pencil top fast between finger and thumb, and let go on the plate. 3. Watch the colours.
flow.say: First try to stand it up without spinning. What happens? Now spin it hard. What colour do you see while it spins?
flow.kid: Stand it still. Does it fall? Now spin it. What colour do you see?

good: They went orange.
The red and yellow mixed together.

flow.parent: Still, the top falls over at once. Spinning, it stands up. The red and yellow look orange because the eye sees them one after the other, too fast to tell apart. Try a dot near the edge too: it looks like a ring.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a question about your top.
flow.kid: Answer this one.

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl aged seven, colours half her top red and half yellow. What colour will she see while it spins fast?
check.why: Spinning fast mixes the red and yellow in the eye, so the top looks orange.

challenges.title: Make the Cup Roll Straight
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A paper cup always curves round when it rolls. Your job is to make it roll straight to a doll or a teddy across the room.
challenges.problem: Divya wants to send a paper cup rolling straight to her teddy, three steps away. But the cup keeps curving round. How can she make it roll straight?
constraints: The cup must roll, not slide.
You may use paper cups, tape and paper.
Let go from the same slope each time.
materials: 2 or 3 paper cups or plastic cups
the tray-and-books slope from the slope test
general: Wheels on a car are all the same size, so the car goes straight.
A bottle is the same width at both ends, so it rolls straight.
creative: Tape two cups together, wide end to wide end.
Tape two cups narrow end to narrow end.
Roll a sheet of paper into a tube and slip the cup inside it, so the outside is the same width all along.
challenges.your_turn: Find one way to make the cup roll straight. Draw it, and say what you changed.

setup.art: A paper cup curving off to one side on the floor, away from a teddy sitting three steps away.
setup.caption: 1. The cup curves away from the teddy.

setup.art: Two paper cups taped wide end to wide end, rolling straight to the teddy.
setup.caption: 2. Change the cup so it rolls straight.

flow.do: Read the problem. Sit the teddy three steps from the slope. Roll one cup to show how it curves.
flow.say: The cup curves away from the teddy. Why does it curve? How could you make it go straight?
flow.kid: The cup curves. How can you make it go straight?

good: One end is big and one is small.
The wide end goes further.

flow.do: Your child tries their ideas. Help with taping only if asked.
flow.say: Try your idea. Did it roll straight? What could you change?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Did it go straight? Change it and try again.
flow.parent: Two cups taped wide end to wide end, or narrow end to narrow end, roll straight. Both ends are now the same.

flow.do: Ask which idea worked best, and why. Then the check question.
flow.say: Which idea worked? Why did it go straight?
flow.kid: Which idea worked? Why?

check.q: Why do two cups taped wide end to wide end roll straight?
options: Both ends are now the same width
check.why: Both ends now go the same distance on each turn, so nothing turns them to the side.

items.p: Will it roll or stay still on a slope? A grown-up reads each one. Circle the rollers in red and the stay-stills in blue.
items.why: Round things roll. Things with flat sides stay still, or slide if the slope is steep. A strong answer says round or flat.

items.p: A toy cart has one big wheel and one small wheel on the same bar. Which way does it go when you push it?
opts: It does not move at all
items.why: The big wheel goes further on each turn than the small one, so the cart turns, just as the paper cup does.

items.p: Draw a toy that rolls. Colour the round parts that touch the ground.
items.a: A toy with round parts touching the ground, such as a car with wheels or a ball.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the parts touching the ground are round.

items.p: Draw a line from each toy to how it moves.
items.why: A ball bounces, a top spins round its middle, a car rolls on round wheels, and a doll on a slide keeps the same side down and slides.
items.art: A ball, a top, a toy car and a doll on a slide on the left, and four small arrows showing bounce, spin, roll and slide on the right.

items.p: A ball dropped from high up bounces higher than a ball dropped from low down.
items.why: True. In the drop test, the shoulder drop gave a higher bounce than the knee drop.

items.p: Three of these roll. Which one does not?
items.why: The book has flat sides, so it does not roll. The ball, the bangle and the orange are round where they touch the ground.

items.p: A box and a bottle are put at the top of the same slope. Say why the bottle can roll and the box cannot. Say it out loud and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The box has flat sides. The bottle is round, so it can turn over and over.
items.why: A strong answer says the bottle is round and the box is flat.

items.p: Lakshmi and her friend Zainab watched the paper cup curve round on the floor.

views.says: The cup went round because of its shape. One end is wide and one end is narrow.
No, the floor made it go round. On a slippery floor it would just slide.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right. Say it out loud and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For Lakshmi: the bottle rolled straight on the same floor, so the shape made the difference. For Zainab: the floor's grip holds the two ends as they roll. On a very slippery floor the cup would slide, not roll.
items.why: Both children see something true. The shape decides which way the cup turns, and the floor's grip, called friction, is what lets it roll at all.

items.p: Look at the toy car with its inside showing. A grown-up points to each part. Say what it is, and the grown-up writes it.
items.why: Turning the key winds the spring. The spring unwinds and turns the wheels, and the round wheels roll.
items.art: A cut-away wind-up toy car showing round wheels, a coiled spring inside joined to the wheels, and a key on the side, each with an empty label.

items.p: Why does a wind-up toy stop after a while?
opts: Its spring has unwound all the way
items.why: The toy moves only while the spring unwinds. When the spring has given back all your winding, the toy stops. Wind it again to go again.

items.p: A child drops a ball once on a soft pillow and once on hard tiles. Where does it bounce higher?
items.why: A hard floor sends the ball back up. A soft pillow squashes and does not push back, so the ball hardly bounces.

items.p: A heavy book was hard to push. Then it sat on round pencils, and it was easy to push. Why? Say it out loud and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The pencils are round, so they rolled, and the book rode along on top.
items.why: A strong answer says the pencils rolled because they are round.

items.p: Put the twisting sock in order, from first to last. A grown-up reads each one.
items: The sock slows down and stops
a: The sock slows down and stops
items.why: First the twist stores your push in the string. When you let go, the string untwists and spins the sock, until the twist is used up.

items.p: Draw the path a bottle makes when it rolls on the floor. Then draw the path a paper cup makes.
items.a: A straight line for the bottle and a curved line, part of a circle, for the cup.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bottle going straight and the cup curving round.

items.p: A top spins for longer on a smooth plate than on a rough mat. Why?
opts: There is less rubbing on the plate
items.why: Rubbing, called friction, slows a spinning top. A smooth plate rubs less than a rough mat, so the top spins for longer.

items.p: Which ones bounce well, and which hardly bounce? A grown-up reads each one. Put a tick for bounces well and a cross for hardly bounces.
items: A ball of wet atta dough
items.why: A ball bounces well if it springs back into shape after it squashes. Dough and socks squash and stay soft, so they hardly bounce.

items.p: Divya and Zeenat are watching a top spin on a steel plate in Hyderabad.

views.says: The top stands up because it is spinning.
The top stands up because its point is sharp.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right. Say it out loud and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For Divya: the same top with the same point fell over when it was still, so the spin is what holds it up. For Zeenat: a sharp, smooth point rubs less on the plate, so the top keeps spinning longer.
items.why: Divya has the main reason: spinning keeps a top up. Zeenat is right that the point matters, because a point that rubs less lets the top spin for longer.

items.p: Which of these gets its push from a spring inside?
items.why: Turning the key winds a spring inside the car. The spring unwinds and turns the wheels.

items.p: Look at the three pictures of a bouncing ball. A grown-up points to each picture. Say what is happening, and the grown-up writes it.
labels: the ball squashes on the floor
the ball springs back and goes up
items.why: A bounce has three parts: the fall, the squash, and the spring back that sends the ball up.
items.art: Three pictures of one ball in a row: falling down, squashed flat on the floor, and round again going up, each with an empty label.

items.p: Think of a new toy that rolls, bounces or spins. Say what it looks like and what push or pull starts it moving. A grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Any toy, with a clear way it moves and what starts it, such as 'a spinning flower top that I start by twisting it with my fingers'.
items.why: A strong answer names the move, roll, bounce or spin, and the push or pull that starts it.

quiz.p: Which of these will roll down a slope?
opts: A round bottle on its side
quiz.why: The bottle is round where it touches the slope, so it rolls. The book and the box have flat sides.

quiz.p: A girl lets go of a box at the top of a gentle slope. What will it most likely do?
quiz.why: A box has flat sides, so on a gentle slope it stays still. On a steep slope it may slide.

quiz.p: A paper cup rolls on the floor. Why does it curve round?
opts: Its wide end goes further on each turn than its narrow end
quiz.why: On each turn, the wide end goes a long way and the narrow end a short way, so the cup turns.

quiz.p: Which of these will roll straight?
opts: A bottle, the same width at both ends
quiz.why: A thing the same width all along rolls straight. A cup or a cone curves round.

quiz.p: What happens to a rubber ball when it hits the floor?
opts: It squashes a little, then springs back
quiz.why: A ball squashes for a moment and springs back into shape. That spring back sends it up.

quiz.p: A ball is dropped and bounces three times. How does each bounce compare with the one before?
quiz.why: A ball loses some movement on each bounce, to sound and warmth. So each bounce is lower, until the ball stops.

quiz.p: When can a top stand up on its point?
quiz.why: A spinning top stands up on its point. When it stops spinning, it falls over.

quiz.p: Why does a spinning top slow down and fall in the end?
opts: Its point rubs on the floor
quiz.why: Rubbing at the point, called friction, slowly uses up the spin. Then the top wobbles and falls.

quiz.p: What is inside a wind-up toy that keeps your winding?
quiz.why: Turning the key winds a metal spring tight. The spring unwinds and turns the wheels.

quiz.p: A ball rolls down a slope and nobody pushes it. What started it moving?
quiz.why: The slope started it. Every toy starts moving with a push or a pull, from a hand, a foot, a slope or a spring.

videos.why: Shows real toy makers in Karnataka shaping wooden toys on a spinning lathe.
videos.check: Found by search: "How Channapatna’s 200-year-old toy making craft is bouncing back from the edge of death" by The News Minute, 6 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: A tennis ball bounce in slow motion
videos.why: In slow motion you can see the ball squash flat on the floor and spring back up.
videos.check: Found by search: "The Beauty of Slow Motion - Tennis Ball Bounce" by ScienceLuxembourg, 21 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Bottle spinner made from waste
videos.why: Arvind Gupta, an Indian toy maker and science teacher, shows how to make a spinning toy from things people throw away.
videos.check: Found by search: "Bottle Spinner | English" by Arvind Gupta, 2 minutes 49 seconds. A parent may preview it.

applications: Every car, bus, auto and cycle rolls on round wheels.
Tiny steel balls, called ball bearings, roll inside cycle wheels and fans so they turn easily.
A potter's wheel spins round its middle while the potter shapes a pot.
A washing machine spins the clothes fast to throw the water out.
In 2017, Manu Prakash's team at Stanford University made a paper spinner, like a button on a string, that spins blood to help test for malaria where there is no electricity.

spotted.art: A stall of bright lacquered wooden tops and pull-along toys at a fair.

spotted.text: Children in Madurai playing with a string top, a pambaram, on a flat terrace.
spotted.art: Two girls on a terrace, one winding a string round a wooden top, the other watching a top spin.

spotted.text: A potter in Khurja or Kumartuli spinning a wheel to shape a clay pot.
spotted.art: A woman potter's hands shaping a clay pot on a spinning wheel.

spotted.text: A child rolling an old cycle tyre along a lane with a stick in a Goa village.
spotted.art: A girl running beside an old cycle tyre, keeping it rolling with a stick.

spotted.text: The giant wheel at a Durga Puja mela in Kolkata, spinning round its middle.
spotted.art: A lit-up giant wheel at night at a crowded mela.

open_questions.q: Who made the very first spinning top?
open_questions.why_open: Tops have been found in very old places in many parts of the world. Nobody knows who made the first one, or whether people in different places each made their own.

open_questions.q: What is the simplest way to explain why a spinning top stays up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can work it out exactly with maths. But teachers and scientists still argue about the clearest way to explain it without the maths.

open_questions.q: How bouncy could a ball ever be made?
open_questions.why_open: Every ball loses a little movement on each bounce. Scientists keep making springier materials, and nobody knows how close to a perfect bounce they can get.

ask_kids: Which of your toys roll, and which spin?
Can you find three round things in the kitchen that would roll?
Why are wheels round, and not square?
What makes a ball stop bouncing in the end?
What spins round in our home?
How could you make a toy move without touching it?

jokes.j: Why did the ball go to the doctor?
jokes.a: It was feeling a bit flat!

jokes.j: What did the top say when it got dizzy?
What did the paper cup say to the bottle?
jokes.a: You go straight. I'll come round later!

jokes.j: Why did the wheel win the race?
What did the floor say to the bouncing ball?
Why did the wind-up toy win a prize?
Why was the top so good at parties?
jokes.a: It always knew how to spin a story!

jokes.j: Why did the ball go to school?
jokes.a: To get a little more well-rounded!

maths.problem: In the slope test, a girl tried 8 things. 3 of them rolled. How many did not roll?
maths.explain: Start at 8 and take away the 3 that rolled: 7, 6, 5. So 5 things did not roll.
maths.context: This is about the slope test, where you let go of things at the top of a tray.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the rollers from all the things tells us how many stayed or slid.

maths.problem: Which of these shapes will roll: a ball, a cube like a dice, or a tin can on its side? Which will not?
maths.answer: The ball and the tin can roll. The cube does not.
maths.explain: A ball is a sphere, round all over, so it rolls any way. A tin can is a cylinder, round on its curved side, so it rolls on that side. A cube has only flat faces, so it does not roll.
maths.context: This is about the slope test, and the solid shapes you know.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the solid shapes tells us before we test which things will roll.

roots.context: We have rolled things down a slope, bounced a ball, twisted a string and spun a top. Now we ask what the curving paper cup tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The bottle and the paper cup rolled down the same slope. The bottle went straight, but the cup curved round. The cup's wide end travels further on each turn than its narrow end. So a rolling thing's own shape steers its path.
deep_truth.habit: We think a thing simply goes where it is pushed. The slope pushed the bottle and the cup the same way, and the cup still turned. How a thing is made decides where a push takes it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the slope test, the bottle and the cup were let go at the same place on the same slope. The bottle rolled straight on, and the cup curved round in a circle. Two cups taped wide end to wide end rolled straight.

three.who_am_i: Your body has its own shape, as the cup does. The same push does not move you and your friend in the same way.
three.what_is_life: Living beings move in their own ways too. A snail glides, a crow hops, a winged seed spins down from a tree, and you roll on the mat.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of round things that roll and spin, from balls and wheels to the Earth, which spins like a top.

roots.thread: The same slope started the ball, the bottle, the book and the cup. Each went its own way, because each is made differently. Everything is conscious in its own way, the cup and the slope too. Many scientists say only living beings with nerves are conscious, and this is still argued.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at one hub. It is the empty hole in the middle that makes the wheel useful.
teachings.link: A wheel and a top both turn round their middle. Your colour top spun round the pencil at its centre. The middle of a spinning top hardly moves, while its edge races round.

teachings.source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (a Buddhist text)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha's first teaching is called setting the wheel rolling. The text says that once the wheel was set rolling, nobody could stop it.
teachings.link: People chose a rolling wheel as a picture of something that, once started, keeps going. In our tests, a push started each thing, and its own shape and the floor decided how far and which way it went.

science.text: A cone, or a cup shaped like part of a cone, always rolls round in a circle about its narrow end. Its wide end covers more ground on each turn.
A dropped ball never bounces back as high as it fell from. On each bounce, some of its movement turns into sound and warmth.

other_view.view: The shape alone does not steer the cup. The floor's grip, called friction, holds both ends as they roll, so the wide end runs ahead. On a floor as slippery as ice, the cup would slide and not turn at all. So the path comes from the shape and the floor together.

practice.title: The still middle
practice.say: Sit comfortably and rest one hand open on your knee. With one finger of the other hand, slowly draw a circle on your palm. Go round three times. Now draw it smaller and smaller, until your finger rests in the middle. Keep it still there. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Your finger went round and round, and now it rests at the still middle. Which part of a spinning top moves least?
practice.kid: Rest one hand open. Draw slow circles on it with a finger. Make them smaller and smaller. Stop in the middle. Breathe in and out slowly.

ask: The same slope sent the bottle straight and the cup round. Is the path in the slope, or in the thing?
If two children get the same push, why might they go different ways?
The Earth spins like a top. Which part of the Earth moves least?

how_we_found_out.story: A spinning top looks simple, but working out exactly how it wobbles is very hard. In the 1750s, the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler worked out one kind of spinning body. In 1788, Joseph-Louis Lagrange worked out the ordinary toy top. After that, for about 100 years, nobody could work out a new kind. Sofia Kovalevskaya grew up in Russia, where universities did not let women study. Many people then thought women could not do hard mathematics. She went to Germany. The University of Berlin would not let her into its classes either, so the mathematician Karl Weierstrass taught her in private lessons. In 1888, the French Academy of Sciences held a prize contest about spinning bodies. Each entry was sent in without a name, so the judges did not know who wrote it. Kovalevskaya's entry worked out a new kind of top. The judges thought it was so good that they raised the prize money from 3,000 to 5,000 francs. Mathematicians still call it the Kovalevskaya top.
how_we_found_out.who: Leonhard Euler, a Swiss mathematician; Joseph-Louis Lagrange, a mathematician in Italy and France; Sofia Kovalevskaya, a Russian mathematician; Karl Weierstrass, a German mathematician
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought women could not do hard mathematics, and universities in Russia and Berlin kept women out. Kovalevskaya's entry, judged without her name, solved a problem about spinning tops that had stood for about 100 years, and won the prize.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 5.2 How toys work: toys that roll, bounce, spin and wind up, and what push or pull starts each one.
science: Rolling of a cone or truncated cone: the cup rolls about its apex because the radius, and so the distance travelled per turn, is larger at the wide end.
Coefficient of restitution: a dropped ball rebounds to less than its drop height, losing energy to sound, heat and vibration in each impact.
Spin stability of a top: angular momentum keeps the axis steady while the top spins fast; friction at the tip slows it until it falls.

quiz: A ball rolls because it is round where it touches the floor.
Round things can turn over and over. That is what rolling is.
A flat book rolls down a gentle slope like a ball.
A thing with a flat side stays still. It only slides if the slope is steep.
A paper cup that is wider at one end rolls round in a curve.
The cup turns towards its narrow end, so its own shape steers it.
A bottle that is the same width all along rolls in a curve.
A thing with the same width all along rolls straight.
A ball squashes a little when it hits the floor, then springs back up.
Springing back into its round shape pushes the ball up again.
The heavier the ball, the higher it bounces.
A light rubber ball bounces high. A heavy ball of wet dough does not bounce. What it is made of matters.
A top stands up on its point only while it spins fast.
When the top slows down and stops spinning, it falls over.
A spinning top stays up because the air holds it.
It stays up because it spins. Spinning wheels keep spacecraft steady in space, where there is no air.
A wind-up toy moves all by itself, with no push at all.
You give it a push when you wind it. The spring keeps that push until it unwinds.
Rubbing against the floor and air slows down every rolling and spinning thing.
This rubbing is called friction. It is why a rolling ball stops.
odd: Ball, marble and wheel are round where they touch the ground, so they roll. A flat book cannot roll.
Rubber balls, springs and sponges squash and then spring back. A stone does not squash.
The first three keep your push stored in a twist or stretch. A stone on a table stores nothing.
The first three stay up only while they are moving. A cup stands up even when it is still.
Bottle, pencil and tin can are the same width all along, so they roll straight. A cup rolls in a curve.
